title: Man Utd hired Omar Berrada to take them back to the top – can he do it?
content:
Colleagues who worked with Omar Berrada across his 13 years at Manchester City note how unique it is that, through all the stresses and in the most seismic moments, they never once witnessed him lose his temper or be gripped by panic.

At least, if those emotions were present, he kept the flapping underwater.

It is a skill that has come in handy since moving across town from the Etihad Stadium to become Manchester United chief executive in the summer of 2024.

According to people who know, speaking anonymously to protect relationships, Berrada appeared to have a personality that could handle the stresses of an all-consuming job; someone who was affable, a quick learner, universally respected and highly rated. On the other hand, he was deemed a little quiet and not overly charismatic. Less ‘wow’ factor, more lab-grown corporate executive, is how some at City remembered him.

It is certainly not bombast that took him where he is today — a forensic nose for detail, allied with ambition and political nous, did that.

Born in Paris, the 47-year-old is the son of an economics professor and a United Nations worker. He spent his early childhood in Rabat, Morocco, then moved to the United States, and has also lived in Belgium and Spain. In the latter, he worked in the telecommunications sector before moving into football with Barcelona in 2004, where he stayed until 2011, overlapping with City manager Pep Guardiola’s time at the club.

Beneath the polished exterior, Berrada possesses a ruthless streak. That much has been clear ever since his days in the commercial unit at City, a department he was made director of in 2015.

He was perceived to always be ‘on’. Everything was urgent. That readiness to do whatever it takes to get a deal done, no matter the time of day, could create unsociable hours for those working under him. Berrada’s demands could feel relentless, particularly when lengthy voice notes landed on weekends.

Underperformance was not tolerated. There were goals to pursue, but with him there was always a stretch target — and a perception that achieving the latter was what you were truly judged on. One former colleague attributes Berrada’s decisiveness to the business culture of Spain. The mentality there is more black and white, compared to stereotypical British deference — you deliver your objectives or you are out.

Since taking over in July 2024, Berrada has had to play the bogeyman more regularly than he would have liked in his first 18 months.

Tasked with trimming the fat by minority owner Sir Jim Ratcliffe, who had bought a stake in United the previous February and is now in charge of their football operation, Berrada was the person who had to tell club staff he could not promise there would not be more pain in store, just six months after 250 employees were made redundant in the days before he officially started in his CEO role.

This calendar year started in the same vein, with head coach Ruben Amorim sacked on January 5 after less than 14 months in the job. It is the third major personnel decision that the club have U-turned on under Berrada’s stewardship.

They retained manager Erik ten Hag at the end of the 2023-24 season only to sack him early in the next one and paid compensation to Newcastle United for sporting director Dan Ashworth that same summer but parted ways with him after just five months — two decisions Berrada was across, despite officially still being on gardening leave from City. In all, it has cost an estimated £37million ($50.5m) to hire and fire the trio, excluding wages.

Many former colleagues of Berrada’s at City feared that, having wielded the axe at United, the sharp end could soon be swinging in his direction. But people at United, speaking anonymously to protect relationships, claim any such concerns are misplaced. Having been introduced to Ratcliffe by an intermediary and greatly impressing in an initial meeting, which lasted hours, he is the man entrusted with seeing through this transformation.

Last summer’s signings of Senne Lammens, Matheus Cunha, Bryan Mbeumo and Benjamin Sesko are viewed as evidence of improved decision-making under revamped and settled executive, data and scouting teams, despite those other costly setbacks.

Berrada’s hiring was regarded as a coup, and he was considered to be someone who intimately knew what elite standards looked like. But, at the same time, his own specific qualities remained somewhat opaque.

The Athletic spoke to various people with experience of working alongside him at both Manchester clubs to piece together who the man perched next to Ratcliffe really is.

Having spent seven years at Barcelona as head of sponsorships, Berrada joined City’s London office in 2011 as director of international marketing before moving up the ranks to become commercial director.

City Football Group (CFG) grew into a behemoth of an organisation during that time, with over 700 staff worldwide, and Berrada played a key role in adding an important component to it.

A sponsorship with Japanese car manufacturer Nissan, worth almost £10million ($13.6m at the current rate), included the purchase of a 20 per cent stake in Yokohama F Marinos of that country’s top flight. After more than a year working on the deal, it looked like it was off. Knowing how important it was to the trajectory of the business, Berrada boarded a plane to Japan and returned to the UK with the contract signed.

One colleague jokes that he saw Berrada as the Lionel Messi of the commercial world. But football is a different beast, and he needed to earn his stripes on the sporting side of the business.

His status as an ex-Barcelona employee and Catalan speaker did him no harm at City. It was a common riposte to joke about the club’s ‘Catalan mafia’, composed of first-team manager Guardiola, chief executive Ferran Soriano and sporting director Txiki Begiristain. That group were seen as insular by some, so Berrada having one foot in the door was to his advantage.

He found a mentor in Soriano, who Berrada was eventually groomed to succeed.

Berrada served as his right hand and started to gain experience in various departments across the club. This was a sign of his ambition — the rounding out of his skill set to prepare him for further steps up the food chain at City.

His move from commercial director to chief operating officer in 2016 coincided with the appointment of Guardiola. Berrada was more like a deputy chief executive, given how closely he worked with Soriano, who was dedicating more time to building out the City-led global multi-club network. Berrada was viewed as a breath of fresh air as he was more personable than the CEO, and more open to collaboration. He was able to connect with people and would defend his inner circle loyally.

In 2020, he moved across to CFG in the role of chief football operations officer. The worldwide network of clubs had already been established and the group’s football methodology was in place but he oversaw all the businesses and transactions, centralising all decision-making, including at New York City FC of Major League Soccer.

He worked extremely closely with Begiristain, who was considered an excellent sporting director but old-school in his approach to the business and administrative aspects of that role. Berrada took on the responsibility of handling negotiations. It was the perfect marriage, and this role introduced him to negotiating big transfers, squad planning and wage-revenue balancing.

Berrada was ambitious and always seemingly on a self-development journey, whether that was reading a new book or taking a course. According to one person, it was noticeable during presentations that Berrada kept a copy of his CV on his computer’s desktop.

He had received other offers before accepting the one from United. He was courted by several American sports franchises and deliberated over joining an NFL team before deciding to stay put at City.

Berrada felt he had served his apprenticeship at CFG and was ready to take over the reins from Soriano. Internally, it was taken for granted that he would be his successor but when seeking to get a sense of the timeline when this might happen, it became clear that Soriano was not going to be giving up the reins just yet.

Not having the patience to wait until he did is perhaps understandable but to move directly to their neighbours and local rivals, the club City spent years attempting to usurp, stung. His exit was a shock. Yet it was a move that most of Berrada’s colleagues could understand, as few would turn down the opportunity to be the person responsible for transforming one of the biggest clubs in the world, on and off the pitch.

Berrada was not directly replaced at CFG. Instead, Carlos Raphael Moersen assumed the responsibility for negotiations and Riccardo Bigon took over the wider strategic remit.

By all accounts, many of his colleagues were happy for Berrada after securing such a prestigious job. Pretty quickly, however, that turned into scepticism. Some feared the scale of change required may be too big and the attention around every decision too suffocating to succeed. It was the risk and reward of accepting such a high-stakes position. The prospect of making United a dominant force again is tantalising but he was walking into a very different culture from what he was used to across Manchester.

Employees of both Manchester clubs, past and present, paint a stark contrast of the working culture in both organisations.

City are likened to a Silicon Valley start-up — young, ambitious, open-minded. Berrada helped foster the motto of ‘challenge the status quo’, which became gospel in the offices. ‘Best in class’ was another expression that spread, and they regularly conducted gap analysis to try to identify how they could bridge the gap to the very elite clubs, a group which initially included United.

Joel Glazer helped build United’s commercial arm into a machine that became the benchmark following his family’s 2005 takeover, but it has been many years since they were a reference point. City’s commercial strategy used to be about pitching themselves as the cheaper alternative to United, but under Berrada they managed to differentiate themselves. The framing was that brands could choose United for eyeballs, but should come to City for the future. If they were portrayed as entrepreneurial, United were painted as entrenched.

At City, there was a clear chain of command. The line ran straight down from chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak, Soriano, Begiristain and Guardiola. The reporting lines could not be clearer.

Some have the sense that, in his new role, Berrada has had to spend too much of his time managing upwards. Although United’s setup requires consensus on all major decisions and there have been no public spats about the divisions of power, there are many more layers and overlaps in the hierarchy to contend with.

Some observers say they feel some of Ratcliffe’s hires from his INEOS empire can be sycophantic at times and that there is a belief the company’s success in the chemicals industry makes its model infallible, even though their experience in the sporting world so far has been hit-and-miss. Another person found it hard to decipher exactly which decisions and projects belonged to whom, and found scepticism about other departments that made it difficult to feel they were receiving full backing.

People at United, meanwhile, point out that the club has owners from different backgrounds and business cultures, and part of the appeal in hiring Berrada was his knowledge of how to create a modern structure.

The playbook he arrived with is different to the one INEOS abides by. Its way of working is to first streamline a business, then reshape it. In other words: make cuts. At CFG, the default answer to requests for capital investment was often ‘Yes’.

Now he is working for the king of capital restraint in Ratcliffe, where every penny is a prisoner.

Berrada is regarded as exceptional in dealing with agents and clubs, a skill bolstered by him being fluent in English, Spanish, French, Catalan and Moroccan Arabic.

When it came to the summer 2022 signing of Erling Haaland from Borussia Dortmund, he arranged for the striker’s agent, Rafaela Pimenta, to work out of the club premises for an entire week to help close the deal.

It would be difficult to find someone better connected than him in the game, and this means he has intimate knowledge of the transfer market and what United should be getting for their money. He has also been building a relationship with the recently-established independent football regulator.

There were times he had to show restraint, though.

One such occasion was over City’s potential signing in summer 2019 of Leicester’s England international defender Harry Maguire, who ended up going to United for £80million ($109m at the current rate) in that window instead.

There were some doubts within the scouting team, but Maguire was still earmarked as a potential replacement for Vincent Kompany, City’s long-time captain who left the club after 11 years’ service at the end of the 2018-19 season. City’s internal valuations were closer to half the eventual price United paid, so they did not enter into the bidding war. Berrada was disciplined in holding the line and had to communicate the limitations to Begiristain and Guardiola.

Berrada has been joined at United by a host of CFG colleagues, but Jason Wilcox is his most significant choice.

He was brought in initially as technical director, giving Berrada a more direct route into the football department. Wilcox went to United in April 2024, which meant that when Ashworth started there later in the year, he appeared more of an outsider. Wilcox then replaced Ashworth as sporting director after he left in December and was then given the title of director of football, an announcement made privately in an email to staff rather than through official channels.

Berrada also played a central role in the doomed appointment of Amorim, travelling to Lisbon to conduct the talks which brought the Portuguese coach to England.

Though he has worked very well in a clearly defined structure, is Berrada a visionary? Can he be the architect who shapes a club in his image? It was a question that even his most ardent supporters at City could not answer for sure.

The cult of Soriano, a figure who casts such a huge shadow at City, is powerful and has often led to those in his orbit parroting his ideas. It’s become a self-fulfilling prophecy that any hire at City must meet the gold standard, but even those who have spent many years at the group concede it is often difficult to distinguish between who is making the wave and who is riding it.

Michael Carrick, the former United midfielder and assistant appointed as their head coach until the end of the season after the Amorim sacking, is making his own wave at Old Trafford with four wins in his first five matches, including beating Arsenal and City. If he continues this impressive start, Berrada will face the fourth big call of his tenure: whether to ride the crest or not.
